source_title: Steam to Hot Water Transition | Climate Collaborative
evidence: Updating this system will help reduce energy consumption and ensure the long-term resilience of Dartmouth and surrounding communities.

source_title: Steam to Hot Water Transition | Climate Collaborative
evidence: At the heart is an energy plant, which generates heat (steam) and cooling (chilled water).

source_title: Steam to Hot Water Transition | Climate Collaborative
evidence: Transferring steam through distribution piping to heat buildings has been a standard practice on campuses for over a century.

source_title: Steam to Hot Water Transition | Climate Collaborative
evidence: These systems are tried and true, but as we work to modernize our infrastructure, moving away from steam offers a big opportunity for improved efficiency and resilience.

source_title: Steam to Hot Water Transition | Climate Collaborative
evidence: The trouble with steam is that it loses a lot of heat on transfer, meaning that as the plant (the heart of our circulatory system) pushes that steam out to the buildings, some of that heat evaporates into thin air.

source_title: Steam to Hot Water Transition | Climate Collaborative
evidence: For every unit of energy we use to make steam, only 52% of that energy winds up heating the building.

source_title: Steam to Hot Water Transition | Climate Collaborative
evidence: With the transition to hot water, we can enable these heat recovery technologies.

source_title: Steam to Hot Water Transition | Climate Collaborative
evidence: An alternative to pumping steam through our campus circulatory system is hot water. 140°F water loses much less heat upon transfer.

source_title: Steam to Hot Water Transition | Climate Collaborative
evidence: A piece of equipment called a heat pump recovers heat from these diverse sources and adds it back into the central heating system.

source_title: Steam to Hot Water Transition | Climate Collaborative
evidence: Heat pulled from the geo-exchange borefields is also added to the system and, together, heat recovery and geo-exchange help meet the baseload heating demand of the campus.

source_title: Steam to Hot Water Transition | Climate Collaborative
evidence: More Resilient Future in Progress Switching to hot water will ensure our long-term resiliency, but it isn’t easy.

source_title: Steam to Hot Water Transition | Climate Collaborative
evidence: That network of distribution piping throughout our campus is used to carry steam and will need to be replaced to instead move hot water, which requires different types of piping.

source_title: Steam to Hot Water Transition | Climate Collaborative
evidence: That means you can expect to see some new holes across campus — all of those steam pipes are buried in a network underground.

source_title: Steam to Hot Water Transition | Climate Collaborative
evidence: Steam to Hot Water Transition Construction Plan Construction is underway for our steam to hot water transition.

source_title: Steam to Hot Water Transition | Climate Collaborative
evidence: Steam distribution piping will be replaced with new, highly efficient hot water piping.

source_title: Strategy | Climate Collaborative
evidence: We are drastically reducing our energy consumption, changing the way we distribute heat to buildings, implementing new geo-exchange and solar thermal technologies, and transitioning to low-emission electricity sources.

source_title: Strategy | Climate Collaborative
evidence: Reduce Energy Demand We are continuously reducing energy use in buildings through a wide array of energy conservation projects including LED lighting, heat recovery, building controls upgrades and other improvements.

source_title: Strategy | Climate Collaborative
evidence: These projects have helped Dartmouth reduce its emissions by about 30% since 2010. 2.

source_title: Strategy | Climate Collaborative
evidence: Steam to Hot Water Transition We will replace all steam distribution piping with new hot water piping, which is a much more efficient way to distribute heat from the central plant to campus buildings.

source_title: Strategy | Climate Collaborative
evidence: Steam will also be eliminated from building heating systems, in addition to other energy efficiency improvements. 3.

source_title: Strategy | Climate Collaborative
evidence: New Heat Sources Transitioning to hot water enables the use of geo-exchange heat pumps which capture “waste” heat from the chilled water system and transfer it directly into the heating system.

source_title: Strategy | Climate Collaborative
evidence: The system deposits excess heat into the ground in summer or withdrawn in winter via geo-exchange bore fields.

source_title: Strategy | Climate Collaborative
evidence: Thermal storage tanks and solar thermal panels will provide additional combustion-free heating and cooling capacity. 4.

source_title: Strategy | Climate Collaborative
evidence: Low-Emission Electricity We will utilize low-emission electricity sources, through a combination of on campus renewable electricity technology and procured off-site renewable electricity sources, to power the heat pumps, hot water pumps, and other campus electrical systems.

evidence: Geo-exchange works like a heat storage piggy bank.

source_title: FAQs | Climate Collaborative
evidence: When we say we want to reduce Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emissions, what does that mean?

source_title: FAQs | Climate Collaborative
evidence: The internationally recognized Greenhouse Gas Protocol divides emissions into three scopes: Scope 1: Emissions generated from sources owned or controlled by Dartmouth.

source_title: FAQs | Climate Collaborative
evidence: Scope 1 emissions are burned on-site and are considered direct emissions.

source_title: FAQs | Climate Collaborative
evidence: At Dartmouth, these emissions come primarily from heating buildings, but also from refrigerants, fertilizers and agricultural activities, and campus vehicles.

source_title: FAQs | Climate Collaborative
evidence: Scope 2: These indirect emissions are associated with the consumption of purchased electricity and are burned offsite by the utility provider.

source_title: FAQs | Climate Collaborative
evidence: Scope 3: Other indirect emissions associated with Dartmouth's business activities include purchased goods and services, student and employee commuting, waste generated by Dartmouth’s operations, and Dartmouth-funded student and employee travel.

source_title: FAQs | Climate Collaborative
evidence: What are geo-exchange systems and how do they compare to geothermal systems?

source_title: FAQs | Climate Collaborative
evidence: Geo-exchange systems consist of pipes buried hundreds of feet underground that carry water to and from a heat pump.

source_title: FAQs | Climate Collaborative
evidence: For more information on how geo-exchange works, visit the Geo-exchange page .

source_title: Dartmouth Highlights Its Work at Climate Week NYC | Dartmouth
evidence: The week’s programming spanned local resilience workshops, panels on energy justice and the Arctic, and a four-part Irving Institute series exploring the energy transition’s toughest pressure points. “The array of Dartmouth-hosted events exemplified our action on climate—from supporting local resilience efforts to facilitating challenging conversations about the impacts and opportunities of the energy transition,” says Professor of Earth and Planetary Sciences Meredith Kelly , faculty director of the Dartmouth Climate Collaborative. “These events also highlighted Dartmouth work, from student projects to alumni career paths.” The week opened Sept. 22 with a hands-on workshop for local leaders from government and nonprofit organizations, followed by a panel on community-based energy transitions.

source_title: Dartmouth Highlights Its Work at Climate Week NYC | Dartmouth
evidence: Moderated by Sarah Kelly , head of Dartmouth’s Energy Justice Clinic, the panel brought together Jasmine Graham of Mid-Hudson Energy Transition and Mark James of Vermont Law and Graduate School to explore what justice actually requires in practice.

evidence: They contrasted a successful community solar project, which cut electricity bills by around 20% for participants and is expected to return more than $1 million to a community resiliency fund, with another community solar program where participants waited more than a year to see any savings.

evidence: As one speaker put it, trust “takes a long time to build and seconds to destroy.” Following that session, students had their first-ever showcase at Climate Week NYC, presenting research from the Energy Justice Clinic and the Dartmouth as Living Lab initiative.

evidence: Leonela Espinoza Campomanes ’27 discussed her work assessing solar feasibility for an Indigenous community in Chile, work rooted in her own experience growing up with unreliable power access in Peru.

source_title: Dartmouth Highlights Its Work at Climate Week NYC | Dartmouth
evidence: The Irving Institute anchored the week’s second half with two double-panel events exploring what Faculty Director Geoffrey Parker called the energy transition’s “actual pressure points: intelligent grid operations, supply-chain resilience, capital formation, and transmission financing.” The first, co-hosted with SAP, paired a discussion on AI and grid intelligence with a panel on critical minerals and energy security.

source_title: Dartmouth Highlights Its Work at Climate Week NYC | Dartmouth
evidence: In the AI and grid intelligence panel, energy and policy experts described a system built for one-way power flow now straining to accommodate distributed energy resources, bidirectional electricity flows, data silos, and cybersecurity risk.

source_title: Dartmouth Highlights Its Work at Climate Week NYC | Dartmouth
evidence: The minerals panel confronted an uncomfortable truth: there is no clean energy transition without expanded mining and recycling, forcing a reckoning between climate goals and resource extraction.

evidence: The second Irving-sponsored event focused on the capital required for the energy transition.

source_title: Dartmouth Highlights Its Work at Climate Week NYC | Dartmouth
evidence: One panelist recalled standing on the roof of Solyndra the day before the solar manufacturer declared bankruptcy, one casualty among many from the billions poured into “Clean Tech 1.0,” which spanned the period of 2006-2011.

source_title: Dartmouth Highlights Its Work at Climate Week NYC | Dartmouth
evidence: That boom-bust pattern, sometimes called the “solar coaster,” unfolded over three decades to help drive a 90% drop in solar costs, making it among the cheapest energy sources in many markets today.

source_title: Dartmouth Highlights Its Work at Climate Week NYC | Dartmouth
evidence: A companion panel on transmission financing moderated by Distinguished Industry Fellow Abigail Ross Hopper ’93 brought together former Federal Energy Regulatory Commission Chairman Willie Phillips, Southern California Edison’s Caroline Choi ’90, Greenbelt Capital Partners’ Chris Murphy ’07, Tuck ’13, and CTC Global’s Theodore Paradise.

source_title: Dartmouth Highlights Its Work at Climate Week NYC | Dartmouth
evidence: They said that the U.S. has the technology to expand grid capacity—what’s missing is the financing, regulatory alignment, and public trust to deploy it at the speed and scale needed. “The throughline is capital discipline,” Parker says. “Investment without transmission is stranded; transmission without disciplined capital allocation is unaffordable.” Taken together, Parker says, the Irving Institute’s four panels were designed to position Dartmouth “not just as a commentator on the energy transition, but as an active participant—bringing the right people into the room, spurring new research ideas, and contributing to durable solutions.” *** Read recaps of Irving Institute’s four Climate Week panels and the Dartmouth Climate Collaborative’s community-based energy transition panel.

source_title: Elevating Collaboration and Innovation at Climate Week NYC | Climate Collaborative
evidence: Dartmouth undergraduates also will take part in Climate Week NYC for the first time via an exposition of student and faculty research conducted through the Energy Justice Clinic and the Dartmouth as Living Lab initiative.

source_title: Elevating Collaboration and Innovation at Climate Week NYC | Climate Collaborative
evidence: Meredith Kelly , a professor of Earth and planetary sciences and faculty director for the Climate Collaborative, says the events exemplify Dartmouth's specialty in bringing people from numerous sectors together to facilitate community-based responses to climate change and the global transition to sustainable energy. "Climate change is an 'everyone' problem, meaning we need all hands on deck to change the trajectory and design and implement systems that are the basis for a resilient, sustainable, and equitable future," says Kelly, who organized the events with Rosi Kerr '97 , director of the Climate Collaborative and the Sustainability Office.

"We stand out as a leader in innovating and convening the multiple stakeholders in these areas." Resilient Communities Via Local Action The events begin at noon on Sept. 22 with Resilience Action Lab: Building an Integrated Just Transition for Our Communities , an in-person "train-the-trainers" workshop ( register here to attend) for around 60 people from government agencies and nonprofit groups across New York state and the New York City area.

source_title: Elevating Collaboration and Innovation at Climate Week NYC | Climate Collaborative
evidence: The workshop is followed at 3 p.m. by Affordable and Resilient: Community-Based Sustainable Energy Transitions , an expert panel on how to work with local residents to realize new energy projects that benefit everyone. ( Register to attend online).

source_title: Elevating Collaboration and Innovation at Climate Week NYC | Climate Collaborative
evidence: The Resilience Action Lab, led by Christa Daniels , the Climate Collaborative's assistant director for community partnerships, will leverage Dartmouth research and scholarship to help attendees develop practical, equitable climate-resilience strategies that are unique to the environmental, energy, and economic realities of their communities. "Our hope is that the workshop equips local leaders to address the multiple challenges affecting local resilience like flooding, poverty, a need for increased renewable energy, and a lack of affordable and accessible housing," says Sarah Kelly , cofounder and head of Dartmouth's Energy Justice Clinic and a lecturer in geography, who will co-facilitate Daniels' workshop with Meredith Kelly.

source_title: Elevating Collaboration and Innovation at Climate Week NYC | Climate Collaborative
evidence: Sarah Kelly will moderate the panel, which explores how municipalities, organizations, and communities are cooperating to design and implement energy systems that improve resilience, affordability, and sustainability on local terms. "I hope attendees walk away with new tools, insights, and inspiration for how we can accelerate a just transition to a low-carbon future in a way that builds community wealth, well-being, and engagement," Sarah Kelly says.

source_title: Elevating Collaboration and Innovation at Climate Week NYC | Climate Collaborative
evidence: The event's second panel includes Irving's Distinguished Industry Fellows Giulia Siccardo '12 and, as moderator, Miranda Ballentine . "The two panels together tell a coherent story," Parker says. "Digital innovation and physical supply chains are two sides of the same coin, and neither decarbonization nor energy abundance happens without both." The second event includes a discussion on the role of capital investment in the energy transition moderated by Donovan and one about the current financing bottlenecks facing the U.S. power grid, moderated by Abigail Ross Hopper '93 , a Distinguished Industry Fellow in the Irving Institute. "The throughline is capital discipline.

source_title: What It Takes to Build a Community-Centered Energy Transition | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
evidence: That distinction was central to a Sept. 22 panel hosted by the Dartmouth Climate Collaborative during Climate Week NYC on what it takes to advance an affordable, community-centered energy transition.

source_title: What It Takes to Build a Community-Centered Energy Transition | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
evidence: A Panel of Experts Sarah Kelly , head of Dartmouth's Energy Justice Clinic, moderated a wide-ranging conversation with Jasmine Graham , executive director of Mid-Hudson Energy Transition, and Mark James , director of the Institute for Energy and the Environment at Vermont Law and Graduate School.

source_title: What It Takes to Build a Community-Centered Energy Transition | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
evidence: Together, the practitioners, who work across community organizing, legal advocacy, and academia, explored how communities can be the visionaries and primary beneficiaries of their energy futures.

source_title: What It Takes to Build a Community-Centered Energy Transition | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
evidence: What emerged was a set of provocative ideas and hard-won lessons about what building a genuinely community-centered energy transition actually requires.

source_title: What It Takes to Build a Community-Centered Energy Transition | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
evidence: Justice Is Multifaceted The panel opened by outlining a framework for energy justice built on four complementary components: Distributive Justice: Who bears the benefits and burdens of new energy infrastructure?

source_title: What It Takes to Build a Community-Centered Energy Transition | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
evidence: Recognition Justice: Are we acknowledging the unique energy needs, vulnerabilities, and contributions of community members rather than marginalizing communities from energy planning?

source_title: What It Takes to Build a Community-Centered Energy Transition | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
evidence: Speakers noted that decisions about energy infrastructure have historically been made behind closed doors by a small set of powerful interests.

source_title: What It Takes to Build a Community-Centered Energy Transition | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
evidence: While the energy transition itself was described as a shift "from molecules to electrons," the justice component was framed as a parallel shift in power.

source_title: What It Takes to Build a Community-Centered Energy Transition | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
evidence: It requires moving decision-making authority away from concentrated interests and toward the people most directly affected by energy choices.

source_title: What It Takes to Build a Community-Centered Energy Transition | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
evidence: Audience members chat with panelists, including Mark James, director of the Institute for Energy and the Environment at Vermont Law and Graduate School (right). | Photo by Naomi Wade.

source_title: What It Takes to Build a Community-Centered Energy Transition | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
evidence: Panelists offered several examples: One community-based energy transition included a community energy council that meets monthly to set priorities, build shared understanding, and work through challenges via an iterative process before launching new projects.

source_title: What It Takes to Build a Community-Centered Energy Transition | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
evidence: Another initiative launched a community-owned solar project in a major urban area that will return more than $1 million into a community resiliency fund for future climate projects.

source_title: What It Takes to Build a Community-Centered Energy Transition | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
evidence: One example underscored the point vividly: a community solar program in which participants saw only a marginal discount on their electric bills, and only after 9 to 14 months of being subscribed.

source_title: What It Takes to Build a Community-Centered Energy Transition | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
evidence: Right-Sized, Not Scaled Up A strong theme running through the panel was a challenge to the default instinct toward scale. "Sometimes we shouldn't scale up," one speaker argued. "A just, community-based, renewable energy transition doesn't have to scale." Drawing on Amory Lovins' The Road Not Taken, panelists suggested the goal is to bring technology "down to the right size, " whether that means how a household heats water or how a town builds a thermal energy network.

source_title: What It Takes to Build a Community-Centered Energy Transition | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
evidence: Community solar and thermal energy networks were repeatedly cited as technologies suited to this right-sized approach, for example, geothermal systems that deliver heat at useful temperatures, modeled at municipal or neighborhood scale.

source_title: What It Takes to Build a Community-Centered Energy Transition | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
evidence: One speaker called for broadening cost-benefit analysis: rather than measuring a clean energy intervention by bill savings alone, calculate its cascading benefits on nutrition, education, hospital utilization, and food security.

source_title: What It Takes to Build a Community-Centered Energy Transition | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
evidence: Conclusion: A Test of Commitment The panel closed by returning to where it began: the energy transition is inevitable, but justice is not.

source_title: Study Shows Economic Impacts of Greenhouse Gas Emissions | Dartmouth

source_title: On Earth Day: Working Toward a Sustainable Campus and World | Dartmouth
evidence: Image Image 4/22/2016 Body President Phil Hanlon ’77 today announced the appointment of a Sustainability Task Force that will build on the significant progress the College has already made in reducing greenhouse gas emissions and working toward a transition to renewable sources of energy to heat campus buildings.

source_title: On Earth Day: Working Toward a Sustainable Campus and World | Dartmouth
evidence: In appointing the task force, President Hanlon charged the group with spending the next year identifying institutional targets for conservation, efficiency, and the continued reduction of carbon emissions. “On this day, the 46th celebration of Earth Day, we recognize that energy is one of the most pressing issues of our time.

source_title: On Earth Day: Working Toward a Sustainable Campus and World | Dartmouth
evidence: Dartmouth is making a difference through the choices we are making about our operations now and into the future,” says Hanlon. “As we work on the transformation of our own campus systems to those that are low-carbon and sustainable, we know that the most significant opportunities to impact our global energy future will come from our scholarly research and from the preparation of our graduates to be leaders on this critical issue.” Andrew Friedland, who holds the Richard and Jane Pearl Professorship in Environmental Studies, and Lisa Hogarty, vice president of campus services, will co-chair the task force.

source_title: On Earth Day: Working Toward a Sustainable Campus and World | Dartmouth
evidence: Faculty members—particularly those with expertise in energy fields—will be appointed to the panel, which will be staffed by Hogarty’s division and by the Office of Sustainability. “With talented faculty, staff, students, and a strong body of past work, I am confident we can create an innovative, compelling, and dynamic sustainability plan for Dartmouth,” says Friedland, who was on the committee that defined Wright’s 2008 goals.

source_title: On Earth Day: Working Toward a Sustainable Campus and World | Dartmouth
evidence: Hogarty says she is “excited to work with Andy and the task force to create new sustainability goals for Dartmouth and go after more aggressive targets for our greenhouse gas reductions.” The task force will recommend changes in campus energy, waste, water, buildings, food, and transportation systems as well as a timeframe by which targets in each area are to be achieved.

source_title: On Earth Day: Working Toward a Sustainable Campus and World | Dartmouth
evidence: The president’s announcement comes eight years after significant energy goals were set by then-President James Wright.

source_title: On Earth Day: Working Toward a Sustainable Campus and World | Dartmouth
evidence: In 2008, Wright said that Dartmouth would reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 20 percent by 2015, and by 30 percent in 2030.

source_title: On Earth Day: Working Toward a Sustainable Campus and World | Dartmouth
evidence: By 2015, Dartmouth had reduced greenhouse emissions by almost 22 percent through a program of conservation, efficiency, and upgrading energy systems in its buildings. “We have already achieved the first of President Wright’s ambitious goals, and we look forward to aggressively pursuing even higher levels of efficiency and conservation,” Hanlon says.

source_title: On Earth Day: Working Toward a Sustainable Campus and World | Dartmouth
evidence: The task force work begins as the College continues to transition away from the use of No. 6 fuel oil—the heaviest, most polluting form of refined petroleum—and toward using renewable sources of energy, such as biomass and solar photovoltaic systems to heat its buildings.

source_title: On Earth Day: Working Toward a Sustainable Campus and World | Dartmouth
evidence: Biomass systems burn organic matter such as wood chips and plant matter to produce energy.

source_title: On Earth Day: Working Toward a Sustainable Campus and World | Dartmouth
evidence: Solar photovoltaic systems use solar panels to absorb sunlight and convert it into electricity.

source_title: On Earth Day: Working Toward a Sustainable Campus and World | Dartmouth
evidence: One of the newest structures on campus, the Class of 1978 Life Sciences Center is rated as a LEED platinum building, the highest certification in the benchmarking system designating resource efficient “green” buildings. (Photo by John Sherman) Hogarty says energy efficiency accomplishments to date include: Since 2011, Dartmouth has added 300,000 square feet of building space while reducing campus consumption of fuel oil by close to one third, in part through an energy conservation program that has installed more efficient equipment, lighting, and recommissioned heating and ventilating systems.

source_title: On Earth Day: Working Toward a Sustainable Campus and World | Dartmouth
evidence: The life sciences building is three times as large as Gilman Hall (previously used for life sciences), and uses one-tenth of the energy, says Hogarty. (LEED stands for Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design.) The renovation of the Class of 1953 Commons dining facility, which in 2011 was switched from steam to hot water heat, has resulted in fuel savings of about $173,000 a year, a 50 percent reduction in the cost to heat the building.

source_title: On Earth Day: Working Toward a Sustainable Campus and World | Dartmouth
evidence: New Systems Offer Efficiency and Adaptability The College currently produces steam heat in a plant located on about one acre of land in the heart of campus, behind the Black Family Visual Arts Center.

source_title: On Earth Day: Working Toward a Sustainable Campus and World | Dartmouth
evidence: Steam heat is much less efficient than hot water heat, with only about half the steam heat generated by the plant sent to buildings as useful heat.

source_title: On Earth Day: Working Toward a Sustainable Campus and World | Dartmouth
evidence: Steam heat is lost along the way as a result of a number of factors, including the generation process, combustion and inefficiency losses out of the plant’s smokestack, and losses over the five miles of underground steam piping.

source_title: On Earth Day: Working Toward a Sustainable Campus and World | Dartmouth
evidence: Hot water retains heat better as it travels through the system and is simpler to operate and maintain, Hogarty says. “It makes so much sense for us to transition from our 120-year-old heating system to a more flexible, efficient, and environmentally sustainable mode of generating and distributing energy,” Hogarty says.

source_title: On Earth Day: Working Toward a Sustainable Campus and World | Dartmouth
evidence: A hot water heating system run on fuel sources other than No. 6 oil could save up to $5 million in overall annual operating costs, she says.

source_title: On Earth Day: Working Toward a Sustainable Campus and World | Dartmouth
evidence: A hot water based system is also more adaptable and is capable of using thermal storage, geothermal technologies, heat pumps, and other heat-transfer technologies.

source_title: On Earth Day: Working Toward a Sustainable Campus and World | Dartmouth
evidence: Converting from steam to a hot water based heating system will also facilitate the College converting from using No. 6 fuel to using renewables to power the system.

source_title: On Earth Day: Working Toward a Sustainable Campus and World | Dartmouth
evidence: Hogarty says retrofitting Dartmouth’s buildings to use hot water rather than steam heat would take about six years.
